# Research trail: "What if the Moon disappeared?" (topic discovery only)

Budget used: 8 searches; 5 pages read (S1 NOAA, S2 NASA, S5 Li & Batygin abstract, S3 the moonlight review, S4 Laskar
et al. 1993). Two more fetches failed and read nothing: the ADS abstract page for Lissauer et al. 2012 came back empty
(it renders by script) and the index page carrying the same abstract reset the connection. Lissauer 2012 therefore
stays a snippet. The Laskar PDF is a scan the fetcher could not read as text, so I took its three page images out of
the saved file and read them myself (no new download). Nothing was paid for, signed into or contacted.

## Searches and what each gave

1. NOAA tides, Sun vs Moon force: NOAA's "about half" and NASA's "a little less than half" (both then read), plus a
   weather site's "46%" (not used: a non-specialist restating the same thing).
2. Lissauer, Barnes & Chambers 2012: only a third-party summary of the abstract (a moonless Earth's tilt more
   constrained than feared, steadier for backward spin), and the Li & Batygin 2014 paper (then read: abstract).
3. "Chronobiology by moonlight" (Kronfeld-Schor et al. 2013): the PMC full text (then read). It was the richest single
   read: coral spawning, the coral experiment, midges, crabs, owls, coyotes, migrating birds, and a frank list of what
   is unknown.
4. The popular coverage of this exact question (Popular Science quoting Matthew Siegler, Astronomy.com, Live Science,
   ZME Science). They agree on darker nights and smaller tides, disagree on how much smaller ("a third", "under half",
   "50-75% lower"), and give very different tilt figures: from "gradual, not in our lifetime" to "no tilt to drastic in
   a few hundred thousand years" to "10-45 degrees". Used only to see how the question is usually answered, and as the
   source of the legend claim C16.
5. Laskar, Joutel & Robutel 1993: located the paper on the author's own site (then read in full). This changed the
   angle. The famous "0 to 85 degrees" is the moonless case at faster early spins (Figs. 3-4: 1.22 and 1.6 times
   today's) and over the long term. For today's Earth with the Moon removed, the paper reports an earlier calculation
   of 15 to 32 degrees within a million years. The tilt beat therefore became "a measured wander, with the long run
   disputed" instead of "chaos".
6. Lunar laser ranging and the Moon's retreat: JPL's 3.8 cm (and 3.7 cm) a year, a 2021 preprint's 38.30 +/- 0.09 mm a
   year. Snippets only, kept as leads for T4.
7. Dung beetles and moonlight (Dacke et al. 2003; a Milky Way follow-up): consistent coverage, but snippets only. A
   strong lead for the night beat; not used.
8. Lissauer's numbers: a 2004 NASA record said to give 12-38 degrees over 100 million years (authorship unchecked), and
   a Venus study that says nothing about a 24-hour Earth. Snippets only.

## Dropped, and why

- From the review: lions attacking people on dark nights (distressing), blood-feeding vampire bats as the dark-night
  example (blood; owls and coyotes do the same work), snakes feeding at carrion and stress hormones measured in faeces
  (carcass and excrement; not needed). All are content-rule exclusions.
- The Moon's folklore and calendars: religious festival dates set by the Moon, "full-moon madness", werewolves,
  astrology, harvest-moon festivals. Never searched for and never used, not even as texture (the holiday, religious and
  superstition rule).
- Tsunami, earthquake or "Earth flies off" versions of the premise: nothing I read supports them, and they would turn
  the premise into disaster as spectacle.
- The coral light-sensing gene (C06): a hedged mechanism ("suggesting"); the coral experiment (C05) does that beat's
  work better and more plainly.
- Day-lengthening per century and the retreat rate: snippet-only numbers, so the film's brake beat (R7) uses only the
  read fact (a day of about 20 hours, 2.5 billion years ago) and says "more slowly" without a figure.

## Where I was unsure, to settle before the script

- Lissauer et al. 2012: its actual range and how it depends on spin rate. Read the abstract before naming it; until
  then the film says only "later work finds the drift far slower" (Li & Batygin, read).
- The coral experiment (C05) is the key moment of B04 but rests on one study (Jokiel et al. 1985) known only through
  the review, on one brooding species and on larval release, not reef mass spawning. Read the original if it stays.
- Clunio midges: whether the northern populations' "water turbulence" cue follows the tides. If it does, the line
  "even the backup clock is the Moon's" becomes available; until then the film doesn't say it.
- A real place whose tide is already mostly the Sun's (Tahiti is often given as one; that comes from my memory, not
  from anything read). It would make B03 concrete; check it first.
- Earth's path around the Sun after the Moon vanishes (the shared balance point lies inside Earth, so the orbit should
  barely change): not researched. The film should not claim it until checked.
- The tides "shrinking to about a third" is my arithmetic from the forces (roughly a third of a spring tide), not a
  measurement. Real coasts amplify their tides in their own ways, so the film says "on most coasts, much less", never
  one figure.
